subject: Geography
name: Geography, Year 12
syllabus: NSW Geography 11-12 Syllabus (2022), Year 12 focus areas

points.title: What sustainability means
points.brief: Meeting the needs of people today without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs, across the environment, the economy and society.

points.title: The Sustainable Development Goals
points.brief: The UN's 17 goals, agreed in 2015 for 2030, cover poverty, health, education, inequality, climate and the environment.

points.title: Ecological footprint
points.brief: The area of land and water needed to supply what a person or country uses and absorb its waste. Rich countries have much larger footprints.

points.title: Consumption and resource use
points.brief: Rising consumption, especially in wealthy countries, drives demand for resources and the waste and emissions that come with them.

points.title: Climate change as a sustainability challenge
points.brief: Burning fossil fuels raises greenhouse gases, warming the planet and bringing more extreme weather, sea level rise and harm to ecosystems.

points.title: The circular economy
points.brief: An economy that designs out waste by reusing, repairing and recycling materials instead of making, using and throwing away.

points.title: The energy transition
points.brief: The shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy such as solar and wind, which brings new jobs and costs for different places.

points.title: Responses at different scales
points.brief: Sustainability needs action by international agreements, national governments, businesses, communities and individuals.

points.title: Inequality and sustainability
points.brief: Poorer countries and communities often face the worst effects of environmental change while having caused the least of it.

points.title: Defining urban and rural places
points.brief: Urban places have high population density and mostly non-farm jobs. Rural places have lower density and more land used for farming or nature.

points.title: Urban growth
points.brief: Cities grow through natural increase and migration from rural areas and overseas, spreading outwards and upwards.

points.title: Megacities
points.brief: Cities of more than 10 million people, most now in Asia, Africa and Latin America, with large informal settlements in some.

points.title: Suburbanisation and urban sprawl
points.brief: Cities spread outwards as people move to new suburbs, which uses farmland and increases car travel.

points.title: Urban renewal and gentrification
points.brief: Old areas are redeveloped, and wealthier residents move in. Prices rise and long-term residents can be pushed out.

points.title: Liveability
points.brief: How good a place is to live, judged by housing, transport, safety, services, green space and the environment.

points.title: Rural change
points.brief: Farming has become larger and more mechanised, so many rural towns have lost people and services, while some coastal towns grow.

points.title: Counter-urbanisation
points.brief: People moving from cities to rural areas and small towns, for lifestyle, cheaper housing or remote work.

points.title: Links between rural and urban places
points.brief: Cities depend on rural areas for food, water and energy, and rural areas depend on cities for markets and services.

points.title: Planning sustainable places
points.brief: Planners use urban consolidation, public transport, green space and good design to make places more sustainable and liveable.

points.title: Ecosystem functioning
points.brief: Ecosystems run on energy from the sun flowing through food webs and on nutrients and water cycling between living and non-living parts.

points.title: Levels of biodiversity
points.brief: Biodiversity is the variety of life at three levels, genetic diversity, species diversity and ecosystem diversity.

points.title: Biodiversity hotspots
points.brief: Regions very rich in species found nowhere else that are also under severe threat. South-west Australia is one.

points.title: Ecosystem services
points.brief: The benefits people get from ecosystems, such as clean water, pollination, food, protection from floods and cultural value.

points.title: Resilience and change
points.brief: Ecosystems can absorb some disturbance and recover, but too much change can push them past a tipping point.

points.title: Threats to biodiversity
points.brief: Habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, overuse and climate change are the main causes of species decline.

points.title: Extinction in Australia
points.brief: Australia has one of the world's worst records of mammal extinctions since European arrival, mostly from cats, foxes and land clearing.

points.title: Protected areas
points.brief: National parks and marine reserves protect habitats, but they work only if they are large, connected and well managed.

points.title: International action on biodiversity
points.brief: Agreements such as the Convention on Biological Diversity and CITES, which controls trade in endangered species, coordinate action between countries.

points.title: Traditional knowledge in conservation
points.brief: Indigenous ranger programs and traditional knowledge help manage Country, monitor species and control fire and pests.
